# The dispatch simulator — SCENARIOS.md, executable

A discrete-event simulator of the [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](../DESIGN.md), so
the scenario play-throughs in [SCENARIOS.md](../SCENARIOS.md) run as tests
instead of living only as prose. Owner request, 2026-08-13: *"add the 'at
time x — y happens' to the tests, and then execute the simulator — this will
help us make the design more robust."* It has caught two real spec bugs prose
replay missed — **F13** (the occurrence guard's missing closed-at half) and
**F14** (the stale rule can never see a stuck *blocked* item) — which is the
whole argument for its existence.

- [`sim.mjs`](sim.mjs) — the model: a virtual clock and an ordered event
  queue (no threads, no waits, no wall clock), an in-memory issue store, and
  the mechanism as DESIGN.md specifies it — the scheduler run's jobs, its
  drain dispatched only when something is pickable; executor
  RUNS as first-class objects (each drains until nothing is pickable, items
  settled serially — §15.30 — urgent-then-random pick under a
  seeded PRNG, the verified lease, a recorded trigger: scheduler-run-drain /
  label-event / close-drain / failure-redispatch, and an
  `actionExecutions()` accounting of every billed workflow run); the work
  step → hand-off → converge as timed phases with heartbeat comments;
  at-most-once invocation (fired / refused / unanswered); the readiness
  re-check on close; the janitor's rules; and the force/re-queue levers.
  Since #1115 the scheduler run evaluates at the anchor and the schedule
  board is a modeled ARTIFACT — rows the engine writes, a write log, and the
  absent/corrupt/refused-create degradations — never the rule's intent.
  Ad-hoc requests (DESIGN §16) are modeled as their own issue store beside the
  work items: a mark, the scheduler run's adopt job, the built-in request task's
  precondition, and the two write-backs — each modeled where the engine will
  leave a mark, never where the rule merely says something happened.
- [`scenarios.test.mjs`](scenarios.test.mjs) — the play-throughs, numbered
  to match SCENARIOS.md. Each test schedules world events at instants
  (`sim.at('2026-08-12T09:03Z', …)`), runs the clock across a window, and
  asserts on the issue store and event log. Multi-executor contention runs
  through `sim.raceExecutorsAt(…)`, which gives two executors the same stale
  snapshot and lets the lease sort it out.
- [`coverage.test.mjs`](coverage.test.mjs) — holds the map below honest:
  every §15 decision must appear in it, and every test name it cites must
  exist in `scenarios.test.mjs`.

Run: `node --test docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/` (CI runs it — the folder is a
declared test root in `ci.yml`).

## Working discipline

**Change the simulator first.** When the design changes, encode the change in
`sim.mjs`, run the suite, and let the red tests name the scenarios the change
breaks; then update the prose in DESIGN.md/SCENARIOS.md and the tests
together. A new scenario earns a numbered section in SCENARIOS.md *and* a
test here — the number is the cross-reference. A new design decision earns a
row in the coverage map below.

## Coverage — design decisions and mechanisms → the tests that validate them

Rows whose second column starts with **prose** are deliberately not modeled —
the sim cannot catch bugs there, and says so rather than pretending
(see "what the model omits" below). Test names are the first word of the
test's title in `scenarios.test.mjs`.

| design item | validated by |

input.title: The hourly scheduler cron is the fleet's whole Actions allowance — move to a twice-daily tick
input.body:
## The problem

The August usage report puts `claudinite-scheduler.yml` at 1,515 of 2,123 private Actions minutes — **71% of spend** — running at a near-identical ~26 min/day on every private member (MissingBulbWebsite 26.1, WIP 27.0, hitbut 26.0, ClaudiniteWebsite 25.2, EdFringeAllocator 17.0).

Four private members × 24 min/day × 30d = 2,880 min = **$17.28/mo**, which is exactly the $18.00 allowance the report terminates at. The scheduler *is* the allowance, with zero macOS and zero real work. It scales linearly with adoption: WIP and hitbut came online Aug 20–21 and immediately added ~53 min/day between them.

## Why optimising the job buys nothing

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this repo: **median 32s wall-clock**, only one over 60s. Actions bills each job rounded up to the whole minute, so ~46% of every billed minute is already rounding waste.

The cost is **run count**, not compute. The only lever is fewer runs.

## What the 24 runs/day are actually buying

Exactly one task in the corpus is `hourly` — `usage-fold` (`packs/claudinite-growth`). Everything else is `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily`/`daily+1h`/`weekly`/`monthly`/`manual`. Per `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs`, the whole daily family lands at `dailyHour-2 … dailyHour+1`, with weekly and monthly also at `dailyHour` — so a default member's entire anchor set is four clock hours a day (02, 03, 04, 05 UTC).

Two of the three remaining jobs are already solved elsewhere in the engine:

- **Ordering.** The `after:` field shipped (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:184-192`). `growth-extract` declares both it and a `daily-1h` anchor, and its own comment says the staggered hours *"express the same intent and cannot enforce it; this can."* The offsets are vestigial beside a stronger mechanism.
- **Chain continuation.** `executor.mjs:215` is a `for(;;)` drain loop that re-reads the queue live each iteration and calls `readyDependents()` on every close (line 586). A multi-stage chain drains back-to-back inside a single executor run, agent hop included ("an agent session's close-time drain", line 174).

That leaves **adopting newly-marked ad-hoc issues**, `Not-before` releases, and dead-claim reclaims as the only work the 23 extra runs a day exist for.

## The end state

Documented in `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md`; the phased plan follows in a comment below once the design is reviewed.

- Retire `daily±Nh` and `hourly` from the frequency vocabulary; ordering is `after:` only, `usage-fold` drops to `daily`.
- The cron becomes **twice daily** at the repo's existing hashed minute — the 04:xx anchor tick plus a ~16:xx tick that drains ad-hoc work, `Not-before` releases and dead claims.
- 24 runs/day → 2. **$17.28/mo → $1.44/mo**, and a new private member costs 2 min/day instead of 26.

Simulator scenarios quantify the latency this trades away — a full day's work with ad-hoc marks injected, measured against `actionExecutions()`.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md'; s=open(p).read()
anchor = "## Appendix A — the owner's sketch"
assert s.count(anchor) == 1

section = '''## 17. The cron's cadence — two ticks a day

Actions bills **each job's minutes rounded up to the whole minute**, so a day's cost is the
scheduler's RUN COUNT and nothing else. Measured across 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this
repo, a scheduler run's median wall-clock is **32 seconds** and only one run exceeded a minute:
roughly half of every billed minute is already rounding. An hourly cron therefore bills 24
minutes a day per member to perform about 13 minutes of work, and an idle hour — the common
case — pays a full minute to find nothing.

Optimising the job cannot reach this. The only lever is fewer runs, and the cron fires **twice a
day** at the repo's hashed minute (`<hashed> 4,16 * * *`): the **anchor tick** at 04:xx, which
covers every occurrence the calendar can produce, and the **drain tick** at 16:xx, which exists
for the work that has no anchor at all.

### 17.1 The frequency vocabulary

`FREQUENCIES` is `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `manual`. Two tokens retire:

- **`hourly`** cannot mean anything under a twice-daily tick. Its occurrence is the top of each
  hour, so a cron that comes twice a day instantiates two of the day's twenty-four and the
  declared frequency silently becomes the cron's cadence (`S70`). A task wanting sub-daily
  freshness is asking for a cost the cadence is designed not to pay.
- **`daily-2h` / `daily-1h` / `daily+1h`** existed to *stagger* anchors so dependent tasks ran in
  order. `after:` (§9) enforces the same intent, and the offsets never could — a task whose
  predecessor overruns its hour runs anyway. With all four collapsed onto one anchor hour, the
  chain is instantiated by a single tick and `after:` alone still settles it in declaration
  order (`S67`).

A member's declaration converges on its own schedule, so both retired tokens are **accepted at
the door and normalized**: `daily±Nh` reads as `daily`, `hourly` reads as `daily`. Nothing fails
on a stale declaration, and the normalization is permanent rather than a migration window — a
declaration is member-owned data and no vendoring pass rewrites it.

### 17.2 What the two ticks each carry

The **anchor tick** does the calendar work: every `daily`, `weekly` and `monthly` occurrence
falls at `dailyHour`, so one tick sees them all. Nothing is spread across hours any more, which
is what makes one tick sufficient rather than merely cheaper.

The **drain tick** carries the three jobs that are not anchor-bound — adopting issues somebody
marked (§16.3), readying items whose `Not-before` has passed or whose `Blocked-by` has resolved,
and reclaiming dead executor claims (§11). None of these has an occurrence; each is simply work
that arrived since the last look. A second tick roughly halves the wait for all three, for one
extra billed minute a day.

### 17.3 What the drain already chains, and what it does not

A single executor run drains until nothing is pickable (§15.30), re-reading the queue between
items, and `readyDependents` releases a closed item's dependents into that same run. So a
multi-stage chain settles **back to back inside one run** — the agent hop included, via the
session's close-time drain — and a chain's length costs cadence nothing. This is why collapsing
three anchor hours into one tick slips a full day's work by under an hour (`S67`).

**A newly marked issue is not a dependent of anything.** Adoption is the scheduler run's job, so
a mark landing while a drain is in flight is not picked up by that drain: it waits for the next
tick (`S69`). The drain chains consequences of work it has already done; it does not discover
work that appeared beside it.

### 17.4 The latency this buys and trades

An ad-hoc mark's latency IS the wait for the next tick, so the cadence sets it directly
(`S68`, marked at 09:03):

| cadence | scheduler runs/day | ad-hoc wait | cost per private member |

input.body:
Design + simulator only. No engine, pack or workflow behaviour changes — `cronHours` defaults to the every-hour grid, so every existing scenario runs exactly as before.

## Why

`claudinite-scheduler.yml` is 71% of private Actions spend (1,515 of 2,123 min in August), at ~26 min/day on every private member. Four members × 24 min/day × 30d = $17.28/mo, which is precisely the $18.00 allowance the usage report terminates at.

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs: **median 32s wall-clock**, one over a minute. Actions bills each job rounded up, so ~half of every billed minute is already rounding. **The cost is run count, not compute** — optimising the job cannot reach it.

## What the simulator now measures

| | scheduler runs/day | ad-hoc wait | full day's billed runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hourly | 24 | 0.2 h | 27 |
| **twice daily** | **2** | **7.2 h** | **4** |
| once daily | 1 | 19.2 h | 3 |

Two findings worth the reviewer's attention:

- **`after:` is what orders a chain, not the anchor hour.** Collapsing `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily` onto one tick instantiates all three from the same run, and the chain still settles in declaration order — slipping the day's last close by under an hour (S67). The offsets are vestigial beside a mechanism that already shipped.
- **A mark landing mid-drain is not caught by that drain** (S69). The drain chains dependents its own closes release; a fresh mark is nobody's dependent, and adoption is the scheduler run's job. This is the case for a later `issues: [labeled]` trigger, recorded in §17.5 as additive rather than rejected.

## See-it-fail

All four new scenarios were driven red by deleting the `cronHours` filter (every cadence collapses to hourly) and green by restoring it.

`check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, none of the 72 advisories in the touched files; suite 2546/2547 — the one failure is `engine-pack-lane-shims` failing loudly on this sandbox's shallow clone, as designed.

Closes #1225

## What to review

The diff is design + simulator only — no engine/workflow changes. `git diff main...HEAD`. Specifically:
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` — the new §17.
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/sim.mjs` — a new `cronHours` option (null = the existing every-hour grid).
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/scenarios.test.mjs` — new scenarios S67–S70.
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/README.md` — coverage-map rows.

Read `docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/README.md` first for the simulator's working discipline, and `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §5, §6, §9, §10, §11, §15.30 and §16 for the mechanism §17 is changing. Run the sim: `node --test docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/*.test.mjs`.

## What I most want challenged

1. **Is §17's reasoning actually sound?** Especially the claim that `after:` fully subsumes the `daily±Nh` offsets, and that no task in the corpus genuinely needs sub-daily instantiation. Check the real task declarations under `packs/*/tasks/*/task.mjs` and `engine/scheduler/queue/tasks/*/task.mjs` rather than trusting the doc.
2. **What does the simulator NOT model that this change would break?** The README has a "The unsimulated world" section — read it. A cadence change is exactly the kind of thing whose failure lives outside a label-mechanics model (GitHub dropping scheduled runs, cron delivery skew, the `Not-before` grid, the janitor's stale rules whose windows are counted in task periods, `staleReadyPeriods`/`staleBlockedMs`).
3. **Do S67–S70 assert the right things**, or do they assert what the implementation happens to do? Are any of the hardcoded numbers (4 runs, 27 runs, 0.2h/7.2h/19.2h) brittle in a way that will annoy a future editor rather than catch a real bug?
4. **New scenarios worth adding.** This is the highest-value part of your review. Propose concrete ones, with the specific assertion each would make and the bug class it would catch. Strong candidates to consider (verify whether they're actually gaps): a dropped scheduled run under a 2-tick cron vs a 24-tick one (`droppedSchedulerRuns` exists in the sim); a weekly/monthly anchor landing on a day the tick is skipped; `Not-before` releases falling between ticks; the janitor's period-scale stale rules under a coarser cadence; a chain longer than the executor's timeout; two members' hashed minutes colliding. Write out the ones you judge genuinely valuable as runnable test code where you can.

Be adversarial and concrete. Cite `file:line`. If a claim in §17 is overstated or wrong, say so plainly — I would much rather hear it now.

## Deliverables

1. Post your review as a single PR comment on #1226 using the GitHub MCP tools (`mcp__github__add_issue_comment` with issue_number 1226 works for PR comments — load schemas via ToolSearch). Keep it structured and skimmable. It MUST end with exactly this footer, as the final lines:

```
---
_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_
```

2. Return, as your final text, a concise summary of your findings: the concrete problems found (if any), and the list of proposed new scenarios with a one-line rationale each. Do NOT commit or push anything — review only, and leave the working tree clean.

commit 1cf103bc3ffc59e72e57096312f3cc8fc0ae7448
Author: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Date:   Sat Aug 22 12:03:58 2026 +0000

    Model the cron's cadence in the simulator, and design the twice-daily tick
    
    Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a day's scheduler cost is the
    RUN COUNT. Measured across 30 consecutive scheduled runs here: median 32s
    wall-clock, one over a minute — roughly half of every billed minute is
    rounding, and an idle hourly tick pays a full minute to find nothing.
    
    The simulator gains a `cronHours` option (null keeps the every-hour grid, so
    every existing scenario is unchanged) and four scenarios that measure what a
    twice-daily cron trades:
    
    - S67 a full day's work completes on 4 billed runs against the hourly grid's
      27, slipping the day's last close by under an hour. `after:` alone still
      orders the chain once one tick instantiates all of it, which is what lets
      the daily-Nh offsets retire.
    - S68 ad-hoc latency IS the wait for the next tick: 0.2h hourly, 7.2h twice
      daily, 19.2h once daily.
    - S69 a mark landing mid-drain is NOT caught by that drain — the drain chains
      dependents its own closes release, and a fresh mark is nobody's dependent.
    - S70 an hourly task under a twice-daily cron asks twice, not 23 times.
    
    DESIGN gains §17 for the end state: the vocabulary collapses to daily/weekly/
    monthly/manual with both retired tokens normalized at the door, the cron fires
    at 04:xx and 16:xx, and the rejected alternatives are recorded with their
    drawbacks.
    
    Refs #1225

{"id":5221773732,"number":1225,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"The hourly scheduler cron is the fleet's whole Actions allowance — move to a twice-daily tick","body":"## The problem

The August usage report puts `claudinite-scheduler.yml` at 1,515 of 2,123 private Actions minutes — **71% of spend** — running at a near-identical ~26 min/day on every private member (MissingBulbWebsite 26.1, WIP 27.0, hitbut 26.0, ClaudiniteWebsite 25.2, EdFringeAllocator 17.0).

Four private members × 24 min/day × 30d = 2,880 min = **$17.28/mo**, which is exactly the $18.00 allowance the report terminates at. The scheduler *is* the allowance, with zero macOS and zero real work. It scales linearly with adoption: WIP and hitbut came online Aug 20–21 and immediately added ~53 min/day between them.

## Why optimising the job buys nothing

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this repo: **median 32s wall-clock**, only one over 60s. Actions bills each job rounded up to the whole minute, so ~46% of every billed minute is already rounding waste.

The cost is **run count**, not compute. The only lever is fewer runs.

## What the 24 runs/day are actually buying

Exactly one task in the corpus is `hourly` — `usage-fold` (`packs/claudinite-growth`). Everything else is `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily`/`daily+1h`/`weekly`/`monthly`/`manual`. Per `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs`, the whole daily family lands at `dailyHour-2 … dailyHour+1`, with weekly and monthly also at `dailyHour` — so a default member's entire anchor set is four clock hours a day (02, 03, 04, 05 UTC).

Two of the three remaining jobs are already solved elsewhere in the engine:

- **Ordering.** The `after:` field shipped (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:184-192`). `growth-extract` declares both it and a `daily-1h` anchor, and its own comment says the staggered hours *"express the same intent and cannot enforce it; this can."* The offsets are vestigial beside a stronger mechanism.
- **Chain continuation.** `executor.mjs:215` is a `for(;;)` drain loop that re-reads the queue live each iteration and calls `readyDependents()` on every close (line 586). A multi-stage chain drains back-to-back inside a single executor run, agent hop included ("an agent session's close-time drain", line 174).

That leaves **adopting newly-marked ad-hoc issues**, `Not-before` releases, and dead-claim reclaims as the only work the 23 extra runs a day exist for.

## The end state

Documented in `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md`; the phased plan follows in a comment below once the design is reviewed.

- Retire `daily±Nh` and `hourly` from the frequency vocabulary; ordering is `after:` only, `usage-fold` drops to `daily`.
- The cron becomes **twice daily** at the repo's existing hashed minute — the 04:xx anchor tick plus a ~16:xx tick that drains ad-hoc work, `Not-before` releases and dead claims.
- 24 runs/day → 2. **$17.28/mo → $1.44/mo**, and a new private member costs 2 min/day instead of 26.

{"id":5221773732,"number":1225,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"The hourly scheduler cron is the fleet's whole Actions allowance — move to a twice-daily tick","body":"## The problem

The August usage report puts `claudinite-scheduler.yml` at 1,515 of 2,123 private Actions minutes — **71% of spend** — running at a near-identical ~26 min/day on every private member (MissingBulbWebsite 26.1, WIP 27.0, hitbut 26.0, ClaudiniteWebsite 25.2, EdFringeAllocator 17.0).

Four private members × 24 min/day × 30d = 2,880 min = **$17.28/mo**, which is exactly the $18.00 allowance the report terminates at. The scheduler *is* the allowance, with zero macOS and zero real work. It scales linearly with adoption: WIP and hitbut came online Aug 20–21 and immediately added ~53 min/day between them.

## Why optimising the job buys nothing

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this repo: **median 32s wall-clock**, only one over 60s. Actions bills each job rounded up to the whole minute, so ~46% of every billed minute is already rounding waste.

The cost is **run count**, not compute. The only lever is fewer runs.

## What the 24 runs/day are actually buying

Exactly one task in the corpus is `hourly` — `usage-fold` (`packs/claudinite-growth`). Everything else is `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily`/`daily+1h`/`weekly`/`monthly`/`manual`. Per `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs`, the whole daily family lands at `dailyHour-2 … dailyHour+1`, with weekly and monthly also at `dailyHour` — so a default member's entire anchor set is four clock hours a day (02, 03, 04, 05 UTC).

Two of the three remaining jobs are already solved elsewhere in the engine:

- **Ordering.** The `after:` field shipped (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:184-192`). `growth-extract` declares both it and a `daily-1h` anchor, and its own comment says the staggered hours *"express the same intent and cannot enforce it; this can."* The offsets are vestigial beside a stronger mechanism.
- **Chain continuation.** `executor.mjs:215` is a `for(;;)` drain loop that re-reads the queue live each iteration and calls `readyDependents()` on every close (line 586). A multi-stage chain drains back-to-back inside a single executor run, agent hop included ("an agent session's close-time drain", line 174).

That leaves **adopting newly-marked ad-hoc issues**, `Not-before` releases, and dead-claim reclaims as the only work the 23 extra runs a day exist for.

## The end state

Documented in `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md`; the phased plan follows in a comment below once the design is reviewed.

- Retire `daily±Nh` and `hourly` from the frequency vocabulary; ordering is `after:` only, `usage-fold` drops to `daily`.
- The cron becomes **twice daily** at the repo's existing hashed minute — the 04:xx anchor tick plus a ~16:xx tick that drains ad-hoc work, `Not-before` releases and dead claims.
- 24 runs/day → 2. **$17.28/mo → $1.44/mo**, and a new private member costs 2 min/day instead of 26.

Simulator scenarios quantify the latency this trades away — a full day's work with ad-hoc marks injected, measured against `actionExecutions()`.
</body>

commit 1cf103bc3ffc59e72e57096312f3cc8fc0ae7448
Author: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Date:   Sat Aug 22 12:03:58 2026 +0000

    Model the cron's cadence in the simulator, and design the twice-daily tick
    
    Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a day's scheduler cost is the
    RUN COUNT. Measured across 30 consecutive scheduled runs here: median 32s
    wall-clock, one over a minute — roughly half of every billed minute is
    rounding, and an idle hourly tick pays a full minute to find nothing.
    
    The simulator gains a `cronHours` option (null keeps the every-hour grid, so
    every existing scenario is unchanged) and four scenarios that measure what a
    twice-daily cron trades:
    
    - S67 a full day's work completes on 4 billed runs against the hourly grid's
      27, slipping the day's last close by under an hour. `after:` alone still
      orders the chain once one tick instantiates all of it, which is what lets
      the daily-Nh offsets retire.
    - S68 ad-hoc latency IS the wait for the next tick: 0.2h hourly, 7.2h twice
      daily, 19.2h once daily.
    - S69 a mark landing mid-drain is NOT caught by that drain — the drain chains
      dependents its own closes release, and a fresh mark is nobody's dependent.
    - S70 an hourly task under a twice-daily cron asks twice, not 23 times.
    
    DESIGN gains §17 for the end state: the vocabulary collapses to daily/weekly/
    monthly/manual with both retired tokens normalized at the door, the cron fires
    at 04:xx and 16:xx, and the rejected alternatives are recorded with their
    drawbacks.
    
    Refs #1225

    Model the cron's cadence in the simulator, and design the twice-daily tick
    
    Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a day's scheduler cost is the
    RUN COUNT. Measured across 30 consecutive scheduled runs here: median 32s
    wall-clock, one over a minute — roughly half of every billed minute is
    rounding, and an idle hourly tick pays a full minute to find nothing.
    
    The simulator gains a `cronHours` option (null keeps the every-hour grid, so
    every existing scenario is unchanged) and four scenarios that measure what a
    twice-daily cron trades:
    
    - S67 a full day's work completes on 4 billed runs against the hourly grid's
      27, slipping the day's last close by under an hour. `after:` alone still
      orders the chain once one tick instantiates all of it, which is what lets
      the daily-Nh offsets retire.
    - S68 ad-hoc latency IS the wait for the next tick: 0.2h hourly, 7.2h twice
      daily, 19.2h once daily.
    - S69 a mark landing mid-drain is NOT caught by that drain — the drain chains
      dependents its own closes release, and a fresh mark is nobody's dependent.
    - S70 an hourly task under a twice-daily cron asks twice, not 23 times.
    
    DESIGN gains §17 for the end state: the vocabulary collapses to daily/weekly/
    monthly/manual with both retired tokens normalized at the door, the cron fires
    at 04:xx and 16:xx, and the rejected alternatives are recorded with their
    drawbacks.
    
    Refs #1225

 cross-repo contract, and its one real failure mode is a member whose mark label
 does not exist yet, where the enforcer's write is refused and nothing runs.
 
+## 17. The cron's cadence — two ticks a day
+
+Actions bills **each job's minutes rounded up to the whole minute**, so a day's cost is the
+scheduler's RUN COUNT and nothing else. Measured across 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this
+repo, a scheduler run's median wall-clock is **32 seconds** and only one run exceeded a minute:
+roughly half of every billed minute is already rounding. An hourly cron therefore bills 24
+minutes a day per member to perform about 13 minutes of work, and an idle hour — the common
+case — pays a full minute to find nothing.
+
+Optimising the job cannot reach this. The only lever is fewer runs, and the cron fires **twice a
+day** at the repo's hashed minute (`<hashed> 4,16 * * *`): the **anchor tick** at 04:xx, which
+covers every occurrence the calendar can produce, and the **drain tick** at 16:xx, which exists
+for the work that has no anchor at all.
+
+### 17.1 The frequency vocabulary
+
+`FREQUENCIES` is `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `manual`. Two tokens retire:
+
+- **`hourly`** cannot mean anything under a twice-daily tick. Its occurrence is the top of each
+  hour, so a cron that comes twice a day instantiates two of the day's twenty-four and the
+  declared frequency silently becomes the cron's cadence (`S70`). A task wanting sub-daily
+  freshness is asking for a cost the cadence is designed not to pay.
+- **`daily-2h` / `daily-1h` / `daily+1h`** existed to *stagger* anchors so dependent tasks ran in
+  order. `after:` (§9) enforces the same intent, and the offsets never could — a task whose
+  predecessor overruns its hour runs anyway. With all four collapsed onto one anchor hour, the
+  chain is instantiated by a single tick and `after:` alone still settles it in declaration
+  order (`S67`).
+
+A member's declaration converges on its own schedule, so both retired tokens are **accepted at
+the door and normalized**: `daily±Nh` reads as `daily`, `hourly` reads as `daily`. Nothing fails
+on a stale declaration, and the normalization is permanent rather than a migration window — a
+declaration is member-owned data and no vendoring pass rewrites it.
+
+### 17.2 What the two ticks each carry
+
+The **anchor tick** does the calendar work: every `daily`, `weekly` and `monthly` occurrence
+falls at `dailyHour`, so one tick sees them all. Nothing is spread across hours any more, which
+is what makes one tick sufficient rather than merely cheaper.
+
+The **drain tick** carries the three jobs that are not anchor-bound — adopting issues somebody
+marked (§16.3), readying items whose `Not-before` has passed or whose `Blocked-by` has resolved,
+and reclaiming dead executor claims (§11). None of these has an occurrence; each is simply work
+that arrived since the last look. A second tick roughly halves the wait for all three, for one
+extra billed minute a day.
+
+### 17.3 What the drain already chains, and what it does not
+
+A single executor run drains until nothing is pickable (§15.30), re-reading the queue between
+items, and `readyDependents` releases a closed item's dependents into that same run. So a
+multi-stage chain settles **back to back inside one run** — the agent hop included, via the
+session's close-time drain — and a chain's length costs cadence nothing. This is why collapsing
+three anchor hours into one tick slips a full day's work by under an hour (`S67`).
+
+**A newly marked issue is not a dependent of anything.** Adoption is the scheduler run's job, so
+a mark landing while a drain is in flight is not picked up by that drain: it waits for the next
+tick (`S69`). The drain chains consequences of work it has already done; it does not discover
+work that appeared beside it.
+
+### 17.4 The latency this buys and trades
+
+An ad-hoc mark's latency IS the wait for the next tick, so the cadence sets it directly
+(`S68`, marked at 09:03):
+
+| cadence | scheduler runs/day | ad-hoc wait | cost per private member |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| hourly | 24 | 0.2 h | ~$4.32/mo |
+| **twice daily** | **2** | **7.2 h** (≤12 h worst) | **~$0.36/mo** |
+| once daily | 1 | 19.2 h | ~$0.18/mo |
+
+A full day of scheduled work costs **4 billed runs against the hourly grid's 27** (`S67`), and a
+quiet day costs 2 against 24. Scheduled work is unaffected — every task that ran under the hourly
+grid still runs, still closes, and still in order. The whole trade is ad-hoc latency, and the
+second tick is what keeps it inside a working day.
+
+### 17.5 Rejected alternatives
+
+- **Anchor-derived cron hours** — compute the cron's hours from the declared task set at converge
+  time. Strictly better on paper, and the converge already rewrites the cron line
+  (`converge-wiring.mjs`). Rejected because it makes a member's cron a function of its pack
+  declarations: adopting a pack silently re-times the cron, a declaration the converge misreads
+  produces a cron that fires at no anchor at all, and the failure is invisible until a task
+  quietly stops running. Two fixed hours are legible in the workflow file and identical fleet-wide.
+- **An `issues: [labeled]` trigger for the adopt path** — would take ad-hoc latency to seconds and
+  cost a run only when a mark happens. Not rejected on merit; it is strictly additive to this
+  cadence and can land separately once the cheaper change is proven.
+- **A central fleet dispatcher** — one public repo's cron dispatching only members with due work,
+  driving the member floor to zero. Rejected: it needs a fleet-wide index of every member's
+  schedule and a `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` carrying `actions: write` on every repository, to replace a
+  job each member already does for itself with its own token (§8).
+- **A self-hosted runner** — removes Actions minutes entirely, and adds an always-on machine plus
+  a self-hosted runner on repositories whose executor runs agent code with real secrets.
+- **Keeping the hourly cron and shortening the job** — the measurement above forecloses it: the
+  job is already a third of its billed minute.
+
+### 17.6 What this does not change
+
+The queue's mechanics are untouched. The scheduler run's four jobs, the drain gate, the executor's
+claim and lease model, the janitor's rules, `workflow_dispatch` with `wake` as the never-wait
+lever (§8), and every label transition in §4 behave exactly as before — they simply happen twice a
+day instead of twenty-four times. Nothing about delivery weakens: what a lost label event would
+have delivered is still exactly what the next tick's parting look sees.
+

Design + simulator only. No engine, pack or workflow behaviour changes — `cronHours` defaults to the every-hour grid, so every existing scenario runs exactly as before.

## Why

`claudinite-scheduler.yml` is 71% of private Actions spend (1,515 of 2,123 min in August), at ~26 min/day on every private member. Four members × 24 min/day × 30d = $17.28/mo, which is precisely the $18.00 allowance the usage report terminates at.

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs: **median 32s wall-clock**, one over a minute. Actions bills each job rounded up, so ~half of every billed minute is already rounding. **The cost is run count, not compute** — optimising the job cannot reach it.

## What the simulator now measures

| | scheduler runs/day | ad-hoc wait | full day's billed runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hourly | 24 | 0.2 h | 27 |
| **twice daily** | **2** | **7.2 h** | **4** |
| once daily | 1 | 19.2 h | 3 |

Two findings worth the reviewer's attention:

- **`after:` is what orders a chain, not the anchor hour.** Collapsing `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily` onto one tick instantiates all three from the same run, and the chain still settles in declaration order — slipping the day's last close by under an hour (S67). The offsets are vestigial beside a mechanism that already shipped.
- **A mark landing mid-drain is not caught by that drain** (S69). The drain chains dependents its own closes release; a fresh mark is nobody's dependent, and adoption is the scheduler run's job. This is the case for a later `issues: [labeled]` trigger, recorded in §17.5 as additive rather than rejected.

## See-it-fail

All four new scenarios were driven red by deleting the `cronHours` filter (every cadence collapses to hourly) and green by restoring it.

`check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, none of the 72 advisories in the touched files; suite 2546/2547 — the one failure is `engine-pack-lane-shims` failing loudly on this sandbox's shallow clone, as designed.

Closes #1227

This is the design-and-measurement slice only. The vocabulary collapse, the cron rewrite and the fleet rollout are separate slices tracked under #1225.

# The dispatch simulator — SCENARIOS.md, executable

A discrete-event simulator of the [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](../DESIGN.md), so
the scenario play-throughs in [SCENARIOS.md](../SCENARIOS.md) run as tests
instead of living only as prose. Owner request, 2026-08-13: *"add the 'at
time x — y happens' to the tests, and then execute the simulator — this will
help us make the design more robust."* It has caught two real spec bugs prose
replay missed — **F13** (the occurrence guard's missing closed-at half) and
**F14** (the stale rule can never see a stuck *blocked* item) — which is the
whole argument for its existence.

- [`sim.mjs`](sim.mjs) — the model: a virtual clock and an ordered event
  queue (no threads, no waits, no wall clock), an in-memory issue store, and
  the mechanism as DESIGN.md specifies it — the scheduler run's jobs, its
  drain dispatched only when something is pickable; executor
  RUNS as first-class objects (each drains until nothing is pickable, items
  settled serially — §15.30 — urgent-then-random pick under a
  seeded PRNG, the verified lease, a recorded trigger: scheduler-run-drain /
  label-event / close-drain / failure-redispatch, and an
  `actionExecutions()` accounting of every billed workflow run); the work
  step → hand-off → converge as timed phases with heartbeat comments;
  at-most-once invocation (fired / refused / unanswered); the readiness
  re-check on close; the janitor's rules; and the force/re-queue levers.
  Since #1115 the scheduler run evaluates at the anchor and the schedule
  board is a modeled ARTIFACT — rows the engine writes, a write log, and the
  absent/corrupt/refused-create degradations — never the rule's intent.
  Ad-hoc requests (DESIGN §16) are modeled as their own issue store beside the
  work items: a mark, the scheduler run's adopt job, the built-in request task's
  precondition, and the two write-backs — each modeled where the engine will
  leave a mark, never where the rule merely says something happened.
- [`scenarios.test.mjs`](scenarios.test.mjs) — the play-throughs, numbered
  to match SCENARIOS.md. Each test schedules world events at instants
  (`sim.at('2026-08-12T09:03Z', …)`), runs the clock across a window, and
  asserts on the issue store and event log. Multi-executor contention runs
  through `sim.raceExecutorsAt(…)`, which gives two executors the same stale
  snapshot and lets the lease sort it out.
- [`coverage.test.mjs`](coverage.test.mjs) — holds the map below honest:
  every §15 decision must appear in it, and every test name it cites must
  exist in `scenarios.test.mjs`.

Run: `node --test docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/*.test.mjs` (CI runs it — the folder
is a declared test root in `ci.yml`). Naming the folder alone does not work:
`node --test <dir>` does not recurse into it.

## Working discipline

**Change the simulator first.** When the design changes, encode the change in
`sim.mjs`, run the suite, and let the red tests name the scenarios the change
breaks; then update the prose in DESIGN.md/SCENARIOS.md and the tests
together. A new scenario earns a numbered section in SCENARIOS.md *and* a
test here — the number is the cross-reference. A new design decision earns a
row in the coverage map below.

## Coverage — design decisions and mechanisms → the tests that validate them

Rows whose second column starts with **prose** are deliberately not modeled —

## The unsimulated world

The validation review's inventory (owner request, 2026-08-13): every element
of the real platform the model does **not** simulate, why, and what defends
the design at that boundary. A test here cannot catch a bug living exactly
on one of these; anything listed as *assumption* is a place live operation
can still teach us.

| unmodeled element | what the real world does | what defends the design there |
|---|---|---|
| **Cron delivery** | `schedule:` is a request to queue: fires land minutes-to-tens-of-minutes late, are silently dropped under load, and GitHub disables schedules after 60 days of repo inactivity ([github-actions-scheduling](../../../packs/git-github/skills/github-actions-scheduling/SKILL.md)) | late/dropped fires ARE modeled abstractly (`dropSchedulerRuns`/`schedulerRunAt` — S4, S5); every rule derives due-ness from durable state, never from "the cron fired"; the 60-day disable is inherited risk, mitigated as today (repo activity from the mechanism's own writes) |
| **Actions start latency** | a queued workflow may wait minutes before running; the drain is not really at scheduler run+40s | nothing depends on start latency; all deadlines (leashes, staleness) are hours against minutes of jitter |
| **Scheduler run serialization** | two scheduler runs racing is prevented by the workflow `concurrency` group, an Actions feature the sim assumes rather than models | S6 models the *guards* under a duplicated fire; the group is platform config, verified in the migration burst (B1) |
| **REST list freshness** | no documented bound on when a list from another node reflects a creation seconds old | **F16**: the scheduler run assumes duplicates WILL happen and self-heals (close all open family items but the oldest) — S30 |
| **Label API atomicity** | a swap is two calls; no CAS; either can fail or land alone | labels are visibility + pick filter, never the arbiter — comments arbitrate (§6.2); a torn swap's stateless item is repaired by the janitor's fourth rule; modeled atomically here, defended structurally there |
| **Comment ordering** | `created_at` has 1-second granularity (simultaneous claims tie); comment **ids** are server-assigned, strictly increasing | the design orders by id, never timestamp (§6.2); the sim's `seq` models exactly that id order |
| **Claim-comment interleaving** | true API interleaving between executors | modeled as stale-snapshot races (`raceExecutorsAt` — S7, S32), which covers the protocol's decision points but not GitHub's own consistency between a comment post and a comment list; residual assumption: a comment list read after posting includes all earlier-id comments |
| **Body-edit lost updates** | two concurrent body edits: last write wins, no merge | single-writer-per-state by construction: only the claim winner edits an item's body, and only the scheduler run (serialized by its concurrency group) rewrites the board; residual: a human editing concurrently loses one edit — accepted, the record comments survive |
| **Event delivery** | `labeled` webhook events are droppable | modeled only as `eventLost` on creation (S16); every flow is poll-guaranteed by the scheduler run's drain — events are latency sugar everywhere by design |
| **Rate limits / quotas** | API quotas, secondary rate limits | costs estimated in DESIGN §5 (hourly-task churn); not modeled; the burst (B-rows) observes real consumption |
| **Clocks** | runner clocks skew; only server timestamps are trustworthy | no rule compares runner clocks; ordering is by server-assigned ids, durations by server timestamps; anchors tolerate minute-scale skew by construction (scheduler run-quantized) |
| **The invocation wire** | the routine-fire API's real contract, timeouts, the nonce's payload grammar | the *semantics* (at-most-once, the refused/unanswered split, the leash settling the unknown case) are modeled (S9a/S10a/S10b); the wire format is not — burst rows B3/B7 prove it live |
| **Actions variable delivery** | `vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL` reaches a run's env only at run start — a value changed mid-run is invisible to it | the batched drain (§15.30) re-reads the variable **via the API** between items, so only running *work* outlives a hold — never the pick loop (S37 asserts exactly that boundary); the stamp is stub wiring, burst-verified |
| **Workflow concurrency between the scheduler run and a long drain** | the scheduler run and drain share a workflow whose `concurrency` group holds the next cron fire until the whole run ends — a drain doing hours of real work starves the hourly scheduler run | the decoupling wiring (work-as-work review, DESIGN §10): the drain must run outside the scheduler run's serializing group once work may legally outlive an hour; platform config the sim cannot see, verified in the migration burst |
| **Secrets & permissions** | Actions secret storage, env stamping, write-gating of labels/comments | prose + conformance checks (§14 secrets path); burst row B4/B7 |
| **Search index** | minutes-stale, eventually consistent | never used by the design (F11) — the REST issue list is the only read |
| **Real code-work/agent content** | side effects, repos, PRs, sessions | durations and verdicts are scenario inputs; the outcome ceiling and record formats are the engine's existing tested surface |

Fidelity grows only when a scenario needs it — an entry leaves this table by
becoming modeled, never by being forgotten.

# Migration plan draft for #1225 — pending fable review integration

## Phase 0 — out-of-band setup: NONE

Verified there is no human-only step. No new secret, permission, repo variable or platform
setting. The one path a converge cannot push into is `.github/workflows/`, and that is already
solved: `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` (`updates/pack-update.mjs:161`) computes the target and
**withholds** it, and the `update` task's apply stage lands it through the member's own PR lane
(`updates/terminals.mjs:34`). So the cron rewrite reaches every member on the existing nightly
cycle with nobody in the loop.

## Phase 1 — the approved stack (ONE review pass)

All code written before the owner is asked for anything, including the destructive tail.

- **PR A — #1226 (open).** Design + simulator. `cronHours`, S67–S70, DESIGN §17, coverage rows.
  Closes #1227.
- **PR B — the vocabulary.** Split `FREQUENCIES` (what a NEW declaration may name) from an
  accept-at-the-door set. Four consumers, all verified:
  - `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs:25` — the vocabulary itself; `anchorInstant`/`periodMs`
    normalize `daily±Nh` → `daily` and `hourly` → `daily`.
  - `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:100` — runtime validation accepts the legacy set.
  - `packs/claudinite-growth/task-declaration-shape.mjs:49` — the author-time check rejects the
    retired tokens, so no NEW declaration can name one.
  - `engine/scheduler/slots.mjs:23` — a fielded re-export shim; stays per the shim rule.

  Four declarations move: `claudinite-lifecycle/update` `daily-2h`→`daily` (chain head, no
  `after:` needed); `claudinite-growth/growth-extract` `daily-1h`→`daily` (already declares
  `after:`); `claudinite-dashboard/fleet-digest` `daily+1h`→`daily` **plus a new `after:`** naming
  the sheepdog sweeps — verified safe cross-pack, since `liveUpstream`
  (`engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:71`) finds no item for an undeclared task and yields no
  constraint; `claudinite-growth/usage-fold` `hourly`→`daily`, **and its `WINDOW_DAYS = 2/24`
  must move to the daily window or its precondition declines every run.**
- **PR C — the cron.** `hashedCron` returns `<minute> <dailyHour>,<(dailyHour+12)%24> * * *`;
  `converge-wiring.mjs:132` passes the repo's schedule; the vendored stub's placeholder and the
  canon's OWN `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` change in the same commit (the canon
  has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly otherwise).
- **PR D — the destructive tail, written now, merged later.** Retire the door-normalization and
  drop the legacy tokens from the accepted set. Body states that its merge is gated on Link 3.

## Phase 2 — the execution chain (sub-issues of #1225, each `Blocked-by:` the previous)

- **Link 1 — force delivery and read it back.** Drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`.
  *Ready when:* PRs B and C are merged. *Worked when:* every member's stamp shows the new
  `packVersions`, AND its `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` cron reads
  `<hashed> H,H+12 * * *` for its own `dailyHour`. Read per member; a member that cannot be read
  parks the link open rather than passing.
- **Link 2 — verify in production.** *Ready when:* Link 1 closed and one full UTC day has passed.
  *Worked when:* each private member's Actions usage shows exactly 2 scheduler runs for that day,
  and no task's standing item is missing its occurrence.
- **Link 3 — retire the tolerance.** *Ready when:* Link 2 closed AND no member's
  `.claudinite-checks.json`/task declarations still name a retired token — a converge-confirmable
  precondition, never a date. *Worked when:* PR D is merged and the suite is green.

## Notes carried from verification

- `after:`'s cross-pack degradation is what makes `fleet-digest` expressible; worth stating in
  §17 as a design fact, since it is the reason the offsets are fully replaceable.
- The measured baseline to compare Link 2 against: 24 scheduler runs/day/member today.

Plan drafted and held. Here's where things stand while the review runs.

**Landed on [PR #1226](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1226)** (design + simulator only — no engine, pack or workflow behaviour changes):

| | scheduler runs/day | ad-hoc wait | full day's billed runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hourly | 24 | 0.2 h | 27 |
| **twice daily** | **2** | **7.2 h** | **4** |
| once daily | 1 | 19.2 h | 3 |

Four scenarios, all driven red by deleting the `cronHours` filter and green by restoring it. Suite 2546/2547 — the one failure is `engine-pack-lane-shims` failing loudly on this sandbox's shallow clone, by design. `check_the_world` 0 blocking, none of the 72 advisories in the touched files.

Three things the work turned up that weren't in the original framing:

- **Your assumption about continuations doesn't hold for ad-hoc marks** (S69). The drain chains dependents its own closes release; a fresh mark is nobody's dependent, and adoption is the scheduler's job. A mark landing mid-drain waits for the next tick — 11.8h in the probe. The second tick is what caps this, and an `issues: [labeled]` trigger would take it to seconds. §17.5 records that as additive, not rejected.
- **I had the cron wrong and fixed it in a second commit.** `taskScheduler.dailyHour` is per-member config validated 0–23, so hardcoding `4,16` would fire five hours before every occurrence on a member anchored at 9 — every task a day late, forever. Both hours now derive from `dailyHour`.
- **`usage-fold` → `daily` has a trap.** Its `WINDOW_DAYS = 2/24` is sized to the hourly period; left alone, the precondition would decline every run. It's in the plan draft.

The delivery lane is also settled, which matters for the plan: the converge can't push to `.github/workflows/`, but `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` withholds the content and the `update` task's apply stage lands it per member. **Phase 0 is empty — no human-only step anywhere in this migration.**

> ⚠️ Still open: the fable review is running; I'll relay its findings and post the migration plan to [#1225](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1225) when it lands. Not yet done: the vocabulary collapse (PR B), the cron rewrite (PR C), and the tolerance retirement (PR D) — all written into the draft plan, none built. Nothing has reached the fleet.

Comment class: other
Review of the §17 design + S67–S70, as dispatched. Suite run: `node --test docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/*.test.mjs` — 80/80 green.

## Verdict

The core economics are right and S67–S70 assert mechanism, not accident. But §17 overstates two claims — "`after:` subsumes the offsets" and "every task that ran still runs" — and the one genuinely hourly task in the corpus, plus the member-configurable `dailyHour`, are both unaddressed. Details and proposed scenarios below.

## 1. Where §17's reasoning is overstated

**a. `after:` does not yet order the real corpus — and one ordering it can never express.** The sim's cast carries `after:` chains, but the real tree declares exactly one: `packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/growth-extract/task.mjs:27` (`after: ['claudinite-lifecycle/update']`). The other offset-carried orderings live only in comments:
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/tasks/fleet-digest/task.mjs:39-42` — `daily+1h`, "an hour after the fleet sweeps at 04:00", no `after:`. The migration must add `after:` on the sheepdog tasks (cross-pack, which the contract allows — `task-contract.mjs:184-192`).
- `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/tasks/growth-promote/task.mjs:18` — `daily`, "after the **fleet's** 03:00 extracts". This is **cross-repo** staggering: members extract at their own 03:00, the canon promotes at its 04:00. `after:` orders one repo's queue and cannot express it. Under a fleet-wide 04:xx anchor, promote runs concurrently with the extracts, so the same-night promotion path (which `growth-promote`'s own header documents) is lost and every lesson promotes T+1. It degrades gracefully (the precondition's 25h window catches it next day), but §17.4's "still runs... and still in order" is false across repos. Name it as an accepted trade in §17, or give the canon a different `dailyHour`.

**b. `usage-fold` is a genuine hourly task, and §17 never names its casualty.** `packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold/task.mjs:35` is the corpus's only `hourly`, and its header says why: the file is the dashboard's whole past-data plane, "its freshness is what the page's freshness IS." Normalizing it to `daily` takes that plane from ≤1h to ≤24h stale. Maybe acceptable (the dashboard tops up freshest hours from live reads) — but §17.1's "no task genuinely needs sub-daily instantiation" should confront the one counterexample explicitly.

Worse, there is a **concrete latent bug**: `task.mjs:31` hardcodes `WINDOW_DAYS = 2 / 24` — the period + slack, duplicated as a literal — and `task.mjs:64` gates "a session captured" on `newestLogAgeDays <= WINDOW_DAYS`. The `commits` half auto-widens (the signal window is period-derived, `engine/scheduler/queue/signals.mjs:14`), but this 2-hour literal does not. After normalization, logs captured near one tick are ~23h old at the next anchor, so the "session captured" trigger goes permanently dark: a repo whose only movement is unattended sessions that land no commit **never folds again** — exactly the silent-nothing §17.6 claims can't happen. The normalization change must make this window period-derived in the same commit.

**c. `dailyHour` is member config; the cron hours are fixed.** `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs:32` (`DEFAULT_SCHEDULE = { dailyHour: 4, ... }`) and `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs:322-324` validate a member-set `taskScheduler.dailyHour` 0–23. §17 fixes the cron at `4,16` fleet-wide and never mentions the knob. A member with `dailyHour: 5..15` gets every daily/weekly/monthly task drained at 16:xx (up to 11h late, daily, forever); `dailyHour: 17..23` pushes it to next morning. §17 must either couple the anchor tick to `dailyHour` (that is *not* the rejected "anchor-derived" alternative — one explicit config value, still legible in the workflow file) or constrain/retire the knob.

**d. Normalization needs one door, and §17.1 doesn't say where it is.** `periodMs('hourly')` feeds the janitor's stale-ready bound (`engine/scheduler/queue/janitor-rules.mjs:20`, 2 periods) and the signal window (`signals.mjs:14`). If `hourly` is normalized at instantiation but not before those reads, a still-declaring-hourly member's item carries a 2-hour stale bound against a 12-hour tick gap → spurious `needs-human` parks. State that normalization happens at declaration load (task-contract), so anchors, windows and janitor all see only the canonical four.

**e. Check the $ column.** $4.32/mo ÷ (24 min/day × 30) = $0.006/min; GitHub's published Linux rate is $0.008/min, which gives $5.76 / $0.48 / $0.24. Ratios (the argument) unchanged; I can't verify the rate from this sandbox, so please re-derive before merging the table.

**f. §17.6 "Nothing about delivery weakens" is too strong.** The README's own unsimulated-world table says scheduled fires are silently dropped under load. Under 24 ticks a dropped fire costs ≤1h; under 2 it costs 12h (24h once-daily). Delivery doesn't weaken; *resilience latency* weakens 12x, and nothing in the diff — no scenario, no new README row — covers it. See S71 below, which I verified runs. Also §17.4's headline "7.2 h" is one sample (09:03); the honest cadence numbers are mean 6h / worst 12h — the table should say which it's quoting.

## 2. What the simulator does not model here

- **`monthly` doesn't exist in the sim** — `anchorHour` throws on it (`sim.mjs:46-52`) and `periodMs` silently returns `DAY` for it (`sim.mjs:54-57`). §17.1 keeps the token; no S-scenario can exercise a monthly anchor under `cronHours`. Either add it or note it as a deliberate sim gap.
- **S70 tests the world §17 rejects, not the one it builds.** It shows a still-declared `hourly` degrading under a coarse cron — the argument for retirement — but nothing models the *normalized* end state (a declared `hourly` reading as `daily`: one item/day, daily janitor bound, daily signal window). The "change the simulator first" discipline wants that modeled before the engine change lands (S74 below).
- **A whole day's work now settles serially in one drain.** Under hourly the day's work spread across runs; under 2 ticks one batched executor run carries it all, inside one Actions job with a 6h ceiling the sim doesn't know about. Not a scenario (nothing in the model to assert against) — but it earns a new row in "The unsimulated world", next to the existing concurrency-group row.
- Nit: `cronHours: []` is truthy → zero scheduler runs, silently (`sim.mjs:1258`). Cheap to reject or document. And the reflowed `run()` comment now reads "— every hour when it is null (each" mid-parenthesis — worth a tidy.

## 3. S67–S70 assertions

Good: S67 asserts creation timestamps and close *ordering* (the mechanism), not just counts; S69's contrast assertion (the drain that ignores the mark is the same kind of drain that chains dependents) is exactly right; the exact 24/2/27/4 counts match the suite's house style (S65/S66 do the same).

Brittle: S68's `0.2/7.2/19.2 ± 0.05` triple-encodes `schedulerRunMinute = 17` and the 09:03 mark — the true values are 0.233/7.233/19.233, so the hourly case passes with 0.017 to spare, and any change to the default minute (or a mark at :00) fails all three with no hint why. Derive the expected values from the tick instants (`nextTickAfter(mark)`) or at least comment the coupling. S67's `slip <= 60` is fine.

## 4. Proposed new scenarios

## The unsimulated world

The validation review's inventory (owner request, 2026-08-13): every element
of the real platform the model does **not** simulate, why, and what defends
the design at that boundary. A test here cannot catch a bug living exactly
on one of these; anything listed as *assumption* is a place live operation
can still teach us.

| unmodeled element | what the real world does | what defends the design there |
|---|---|---|
| **Cron delivery** | `schedule:` is a request to queue: fires land minutes-to-tens-of-minutes late, are silently dropped under load, and GitHub disables schedules after 60 days of repo inactivity ([github-actions-scheduling](../../../packs/git-github/skills/github-actions-scheduling/SKILL.md)) | late/dropped fires ARE modeled abstractly (`dropSchedulerRuns`/`schedulerRunAt` — S4, S5); every rule derives due-ness from durable state, never from "the cron fired"; the 60-day disable is inherited risk, mitigated as today (repo activity from the mechanism's own writes) |
| **Actions start latency** | a queued workflow may wait minutes before running; the drain is not really at scheduler run+40s | nothing depends on start latency; all deadlines (leashes, staleness) are hours against minutes of jitter |
| **Scheduler run serialization** | two scheduler runs racing is prevented by the workflow `concurrency` group, an Actions feature the sim assumes rather than models | S6 models the *guards* under a duplicated fire; the group is platform config, verified in the migration burst (B1) |
| **REST list freshness** | no documented bound on when a list from another node reflects a creation seconds old | **F16**: the scheduler run assumes duplicates WILL happen and self-heals (close all open family items but the oldest) — S30 |
| **Label API atomicity** | a swap is two calls; no CAS; either can fail or land alone | labels are visibility + pick filter, never the arbiter — comments arbitrate (§6.2); a torn swap's stateless item is repaired by the janitor's fourth rule; modeled atomically here, defended structurally there |
| **Comment ordering** | `created_at` has 1-second granularity (simultaneous claims tie); comment **ids** are server-assigned, strictly increasing | the design orders by id, never timestamp (§6.2); the sim's `seq` models exactly that id order |
| **Claim-comment interleaving** | true API interleaving between executors | modeled as stale-snapshot races (`raceExecutorsAt` — S7, S32), which covers the protocol's decision points but not GitHub's own consistency between a comment post and a comment list; residual assumption: a comment list read after posting includes all earlier-id comments |
| **Body-edit lost updates** | two concurrent body edits: last write wins, no merge | single-writer-per-state by construction: only the claim winner edits an item's body, and only the scheduler run (serialized by its concurrency group) rewrites the board; residual: a human editing concurrently loses one edit — accepted, the record comments survive |
| **Event delivery** | `labeled` webhook events are droppable | modeled only as `eventLost` on creation (S16); every flow is poll-guaranteed by the scheduler run's drain — events are latency sugar everywhere by design |

Comment class: correction

Answered in 372dc50. Every claim, including the two I'm pushing back on.

### Accepted and fixed

**1. `after:` subsumption was overstated — the strongest finding.** Verified: `liveUpstream` (`engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:71`) matches an upstream item in *this* repo's queue, so a stagger between two repos has no declarable form at all. The growth lifecycle runs on exactly one — `growth-promote`'s own header says it reads "whatever is already MERGED on members' mains, so a lesson extracted tonight (03:00) is promoted this same 04:00 run … else the next night". Collapsing both to 04:00 makes "else the next night" the only case.

§17.4 now says so plainly, and moves that ordering to the one knob that still expresses it: **`dailyHour` itself**, set an hour earlier on members than on the canon. A cross-repo constraint belongs at the repo's altitude, not a task's — which is what the retired offsets were reaching for and couldn't hold.

**4. The normalization door.** Confirmed `periodMs` feeds both `janitor-rules.mjs:103` (the `staleReadyPeriods` bound) and `signals.mjs:15` (the signal window). Normalizing only in `anchorInstant` would judge a daily task stale after two *hours* — a spurious `needs-human` park on precisely the members the tolerance exists for. §17.1 now specifies one door at declaration load.

**2. `usage-fold`.** Named in §17.1 as the one genuine hourly task, with the `WINDOW_DAYS = 2/24` consequence stated. Your sharper version — that the "session captured" half goes permanently dark because logs are ~23h old at the next anchor — is the better framing and is what the plan carries.

**6 / brittleness / footguns.** §17.6 now states the twelvefold dropped-fire amplification instead of waving past it. S68's delays are derived from the tick grid rather than transcribing numbers that re-encoded `schedulerRunMinute` and the mark time. `cronHours: []` throws.

**Scenarios.** S71, S72, S73 landed. S73 is reshaped from your proposal: as specified it asserted parity between cadences, which passes vacuously when both sims are hourly — it now runs a cron whose hours miss the anchor entirely (`[6,18]` against an 04:00 anchor), which is mutation-sensitive and tests the real invariant. All seven cadence scenarios go red when the `cronHours` filter is removed.

Your "unsimulated world" call was right and is now a row: a whole day settling serially in one Actions job, against `timeout-minutes: 350`, where the sim's durations are fixtures and cannot say whether a real member's chain fits.

### Pushing back

**3. `dailyHour` — already fixed before your review.** You reviewed 1cf103b; 1afa298 landed ~10 minutes later and derives both hours from `dailyHour` (`<hashed> <dailyHour>,<(dailyHour+12)%24>`). §17 is not silent on it. Independently found, same reasoning — a member at `dailyHour: 9` would run every task a day late, forever.

**5. The $/min rate.** Not changed to $0.008. The figures come from the August usage report's own effective rate — $18.00 across 3,000 private Linux minutes is $0.006/min, which is what the account was actually billed at. §17.4 now sources them explicitly and notes the run counts are the argument. Flagging the list-price discrepancy to the owner rather than silently picking one.

**S74/S75 deferred, not dropped.** Both need machinery this PR deliberately doesn't add — S74 needs the normalization door, S75 needs the sim's hardcoded anchor base parametrized. Recorded as a `not yet modeled` coverage row so they surface with the vocabulary PR rather than being quietly lost.

input.body:
## The problem

The August usage report puts `claudinite-scheduler.yml` at 1,515 of 2,123 private Actions minutes — **71% of spend** — running at a near-identical ~26 min/day on every private member (MissingBulbWebsite 26.1, WIP 27.0, hitbut 26.0, ClaudiniteWebsite 25.2, EdFringeAllocator 17.0).

Four private members × 24 min/day × 30d = 2,880 min = **$17.28/mo**, which is exactly the $18.00 allowance the report terminates at. The scheduler *is* the allowance, with zero macOS and zero real work. It scales linearly with adoption: WIP and hitbut came online Aug 20–21 and immediately added ~53 min/day between them.

## Why optimising the job buys nothing

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this repo: **median 32s wall-clock**, only one over 60s. Actions bills each job rounded up to the whole minute, so ~46% of every billed minute is already rounding waste.

The cost is **run count**, not compute. The only lever is fewer runs.

## What the 24 runs/day are actually buying

Exactly one task in the corpus is `hourly` — `usage-fold` (`packs/claudinite-growth`). Everything else is `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily`/`daily+1h`/`weekly`/`monthly`/`manual`. Per `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs`, the whole daily family lands at `dailyHour-2 … dailyHour+1`, with weekly and monthly also at `dailyHour` — so a default member's entire anchor set is four clock hours a day.

Two of the three remaining jobs are already solved elsewhere in the engine:

- **Ordering within a repo.** `after:` shipped (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:184-192`); `growth-extract` declares it and its own comment says the staggered hours *"express the same intent and cannot enforce it; this can."*
- **Chain continuation.** `executor.mjs:215` re-reads the queue each iteration and calls `readyDependents()` on every close, so a multi-stage chain drains back-to-back in one run.

That leaves adopting newly-marked ad-hoc issues, `Not-before` releases, and dead-claim reclaims as the only work the 23 extra runs a day exist for.

## The end state

`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §17, with the measured trade and the rejected alternatives. Cron fires twice daily at `<hashed-minute> <dailyHour>,<(dailyHour+12)%24>`. **24 runs/day → 2**; $17.28/mo → $1.44/mo; a new private member costs 2 min/day instead of 26.

---

# The plan

## Phase 0 — out-of-band setup: **none**

Verified there is no human-only step. No new secret, permission, repo variable or platform setting. The one path a converge cannot push into is `.github/workflows/`, and that is already solved: `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` (`updates/pack-update.mjs:161`) computes the target and **withholds** it, and the `update` task's apply stage lands it through the member's own PR lane. The cron rewrite reaches every member on the existing nightly cycle with nobody in the loop.

## Phase 1 — the approved stack (one review pass)

All code written before approval is asked for, including the destructive tail.

- [ ] **PR A — #1226 (open).** Design + simulator: `cronHours`, S67–S73, DESIGN §17, coverage rows. Closes #1227.
      *Exit:* merged.
- [ ] **PR B — the vocabulary.** Split `FREQUENCIES` (what a NEW declaration may name) from an accept-at-the-door set, with **one normalization door at declaration load** — not inside `anchorInstant`, because `periodMs` also feeds the janitor's stale-ready bound (`queue/janitor-rules.mjs:103`) and the signal window (`queue/signals.mjs:15`); normalizing only the anchor judges a daily task stale after two hours. Four consumers: `calendar.mjs:25`, `task-contract.mjs:100`, `packs/claudinite-growth/task-declaration-shape.mjs:49` (rejects the retired tokens for new declarations), `slots.mjs:23` (fielded shim, stays).
      Four declarations move: `update` `daily-2h`→`daily`; `growth-extract` `daily-1h`→`daily` (already has `after:`); `fleet-digest` `daily+1h`→`daily` + a new `after:` naming the sheepdog sweeps (safe cross-pack — an undeclared upstream yields no constraint); `usage-fold` `hourly`→`daily` **and its `WINDOW_DAYS = 2/24` must move with it**, or the "session captured" half of its precondition goes permanently dark and a repo whose only movement is commit-less sessions never folds again.
      Plus the cross-repo stagger `after:` cannot express: **set this repo's `taskScheduler.dailyHour` to 5**, so members extract at 04:00 and the canon's `growth-promote` reads their merged mains at 05:00. One line, this repo only, no fleet migration. Add `after: ['claudinite-growth/growth-extract']` to the canon-local `growth-promote` for the within-repo half.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
